children: TGIF, I GUESS: INDUSTRIAL PRODUCTION, LEADING ECONOMIC INDICATORS
Investors staggered toward the exit of a roller coaster week with two mildly downbeat economic indicators to chew on.
First, a report from the Federal Reserve shows industrial output (USIP=ECI) was unchanged last month, following July's 0.2% gain.
Consensus estimates called for a 0.3% increase.
Manufacturing output surprised by contracting 0.3%, a photo negative of the 0.3% increase analysts expected.

"The (manufacturing) drop was reasonably broad-based among sectors, but those which have fared especially well over the last year gave back the most ground," writes Samuel Tombs, chief U.S. economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics. "Some manufacturers likely will find that demand softens as they pass on higher energy prices to consumers."

Drilling down, a 1.2% drop in motor vehicles/parts and a 0.7% decline in construction supplies handily offset a 1.8% jump in utilities, which likely benefited from last month's sporadic heatwaves. Without autos/parts, output would have notched a nominal 0.1% increase.
The closely watched high-tech segment was unchanged, hinting at a potential plateau in AI-related outlays.
As expected, capacity utilization (USCAPU=ECI) — a measure of economic slack — held at 76.3% rather than tightening to 76.4% as economists predicted.

Next, the Conference Board's (CB) Leading Economic Index (LEI) (USLEAD=ECI) unexpectedly deteriorated by 0.1% in August, backing down from July's 0.2% gain and defying expectations for a 0.1% move in the other direction.
The index is an amalgamation of 10 forward-looking economic indicators, including initial jobless claims, ISM new orders, building permits, yield spreads and S&P 500 price performance.

"Four out of ten components fell compared to the previous month, with consumer expectations remaining a significant strain on the Index,” writes Justyna Zabinska-La Monica, CB's senior manager of Business Cycle Indicators.
"The LEI’s six-month growth rate turned back to slightly negative, suggesting a less certain economic environment ahead," she adds. "The economy is still expanding, but growth is expected to slow."
According to UMich, consumers would agree:
Main US indexes turn modestly red; Dow off most
Materials down most among S&P sectors; consumer discretionary, energy are only gainers
Dollar, gold gain; US crude up ~0.3%; bitcoin rallies >5%
